title: The Book of Creation
hookLine: an ancient short book on creation through letters and numbers
last: MYSTICAL STUDY NEEDS SOLID GROUND AND A TEACHER.

lines: GOD SAID, AND IT WAS SO.
cards: On the Torah's first page, the world gets made without hands. Not with tools. God speaks.
"And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." Over and over on that page: God said, and it was so. Words, and words are made of letters.
So a question follows, if you sit with that page long enough. What are the letters doing? Are they just how the story was written down, or part of how it happened?
A small, strange book takes that question all the way.

teach.b: Sefer Yetzirah. The Book of Creation, or the Book of Formation. It's short, and it reads less like a story than a riddle.

First, its opening. The world was created, it says, through paths of wisdom, and it names what those paths are made of: ten sefirot, and the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Ten and twenty-two; the book itself counts them.
You'll meet that word, sefirot, again in a few days, grown much larger. Second, what it does with the letters.

The book describes them being engraved, carved, weighed, combined and turned around, one with another, and says that with them everything that is formed was formed. Letters as building blocks, not just labels.

The Talmud has its own small story in this direction: Bezalel, who built the tabernacle in the desert, knew how to join the letters by which heaven and earth were created. A craftsman whose real skill was the alphabet.
Fourth, the name tradition puts on it.
Some versions of the book end with Abraham, and tradition ties the book to him.
Scholars ask other questions about its origins, and the book itself doesn't settle them.
What it gives you instead is a way of looking: if the world was spoken, then every letter on the page has a little of the beginning in it. Kabbalists would build a great deal on this short book.

how: Sefer Yetzirah is studied as a foundational text of Kabbalah, usually alongside its commentaries, and some teachers begin by having students learn to look closely at the Hebrew letters themselves.

practice: If you have a prayer book, a Torah, or a picture of the Hebrew alphabet on your phone, open it; you don't need to read Hebrew, because you're looking, not reading.

Rest your eyes on one letter and notice its shape, the open side, the closed side, the little crown or hook at its top, then move slowly to the next. Let each letter be a shape before it's a sound, and a sound before it's a word.
